Was not the Duke of Zhou’s instruction to the king in these terms the utmost expression of loyalty and affection? Moreover, the house of Zhou established its state through diligence and toil. From Hou Ji and Gong Liu down to King Tai, Wang Ji, and King Wen, all attached great importance to agriculture. The teaching against ease therefore had a long history. Why, then, did the Duke of Zhou admonish King Cheng so insistently about it? Because the resolve to remain vigilant is difficult to sustain, while feelings of comfortable ease readily engulf one; the hardships of ordinary households…

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
難易怠而天命之精微難測誠不可不夙爲之
戒也故游逸淫樂益尚以戒舜況其他乎以此
爲防後世猶有般樂怠敖而不知求民之莫若
豈非末之思耶
詩
豐水有芑武王豈不仕詒厥孫謀以燕翼
子武王烝哉
李攀龍
同考試官教諭袁　批　聖人詒謀在子孫正所
以安天下也豈有根本未固可爲永圖哉此篇
===
深得詩人旨趣而文理充暢才思老成有識有
養之士也録之
同考試官教諭王　批　意足而不重複句新而
非杜撰且涵蓄渾厚得詩人諷詠之體佳作佳
作
同考試官教諭陳　批　講意不講字正是作家
而文體重厚不涉浮淺尤見務實之學
考試官教諭文　批　詞意俱到
punctuated:
難易怠，而天命之精微難測，誠不可不夙爲之戒也。故游逸淫樂，益尚以戒舜，況其他乎？以此爲防，後世猶有般樂怠敖而不知求民之莫若，豈非末之思耶？

詩

豐水有芑，武王豈不仕？詒厥孫謀，以燕翼子。武王烝哉！

李攀龍

同考試官教諭袁批：聖人詒謀在子孫，正所以安天下也。豈有根本未固，可爲永圖哉？此篇深得詩人旨趣，而文理充暢，才思老成，有識有養之士也。録之。

同考試官教諭王批：意足而不重複，句新而非杜撰，且涵蓄渾厚，得詩人諷詠之體。佳作！佳作！

同考試官教諭陳批：講意不講字，正是作家。而文體重厚，不涉浮淺，尤見務實之學。

考試官教諭文批：詞意俱到。
translation_en:
…the hardships [of ordinary people's lives] are easily disregarded, while the subtle workings of Heaven's Mandate are difficult to fathom. Truly, one must take precautions against this early. Thus Yi admonished even Shun against idle roaming and excessive pleasure; how much more did others need such admonition! Despite this safeguard, later generations still indulged in pleasure, indolence, and arrogance, without knowing to seek repose for the people [?]. Was this not a failure to give the matter thought?

Book of Odes

“Millet grows beside the Feng River. Did King Wu not attend to his duties? He bequeathed plans to his descendants, to bring peace to and protect his children. How great was King Wu!”

Li Panlong

Comment by Associate Examiner Yuan, Instructor: “The sage's bequeathing plans to his descendants is precisely the means by which he brings peace to all under Heaven. How could lasting plans be made while the foundations remained insecure? This essay deeply grasps the poet's purport. Its reasoning is full and fluent, and its literary talent and thought are mature. This is a scholar of discernment and cultivation. Accept him.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor: “The ideas are fully developed without repetition; the phrasing is fresh without being contrived. Moreover, it is rich in implication, rounded, and substantial, capturing the poet's manner of expressive recitation. An excellent composition! An excellent composition!”

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor: “It expounds the meaning rather than individual words: this is truly the work of an accomplished writer. Its style is also weighty and substantial, free of superficiality, particularly revealing learning devoted to substance.”

Comment by Examiner Wen, Instructor: “Both expression and meaning are fully realized.”

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
考試官學正王　批　〔醇雅克實〕
周人興聖王隆大統以裕後而必賛其克君也
夫統有天下莫大乎垂裕無疆也周王遷都以
之其克君也信哉是詩首言文王遷豐之事而
此則言武王之遷鎬也意盖曰君天下亦難矣
欲爲君盡君道是可淺之乎爲業而不爲永圖
哉彼豐水東注澤能生物猶有芑草也况我武
王討安天下豈無所事乎方四方攸同之時卜
宅定居殆有事會之不容緩者則開國承家於
是造端也當萬姓悅服之後重教明義寔惟時
===
幾之不但已者則創業垂統欲爲可繼也故一
傳而子再傳而孫繼體守成宜必奠靈長之脉
其諸居上游以端天下極者可使守而勿失天
之曆數將疑固千載不拔之基矣保邦制治居
然締悠久之規凡夫建辟廱以服天下心者是
用勿替引之聖人大寶廼醞釀萬年無疆之休
也謀詒厥孫矣翼子其即安乎武王之所有事
如此是不爲克君也哉盖君道以遺安天下爲
punctuated:
考試官學正王，批：〔醇雅克實〕

周人興聖王隆大統以裕後，而必賛其克君也。夫統有天下，莫大乎垂裕無疆也。周王遷都以之，其克君也信哉！是詩首言文王遷豐之事，而此則言武王之遷鎬也。意盖曰：君天下亦難矣，欲爲君盡君道，是可淺之乎？爲業而不爲永圖哉？彼豐水東注，澤能生物，猶有芑草也；况我武王討安天下，豈無所事乎？方四方攸同之時，卜宅定居，殆有事會之不容緩者，則開國承家於是造端也。當萬姓悅服之後，重教明義，寔惟時幾之不但已者，則創業垂統，欲爲可繼也。故一傳而子，再傳而孫，繼體守成，宜必奠靈長之脉。其諸居上游以端天下極者，可使守而勿失，天之曆數將疑固千載不拔之基矣。保邦制治，居然締悠久之規。凡夫建辟廱以服天下心者，是用勿替引之，聖人大寶廼醞釀萬年無疆之休也。謀詒厥孫矣，翼子其即安乎？武王之所有事如此，是不爲克君也哉？盖君道以遺安天下爲
translation_en:
Examiner Wang, an Instructor, comments: 〔Pure and elegant, sound and substantial.〕

The people of Zhou celebrated the sage king’s strengthening of the great dynastic succession to provide generously for posterity, and invariably praised his capacity to rule. For one who holds unified dominion over all under Heaven, nothing is greater than leaving a legacy of boundless prosperity. This was the purpose for which the king of Zhou moved his capital. Truly, he was capable of ruling! This poem first speaks of King Wen’s move to Feng; here, however, it speaks of King Wu’s move to Hao. Its meaning is, broadly, as follows: ruling all under Heaven is difficult indeed. If one wishes to be a ruler and fulfill the way of rulership, can one treat it lightly? Would one establish an enterprise without planning for its perpetuity? The Feng River flows eastward, and its beneficent waters nourish living things—even the qi grass grows there. How much more, then, must our King Wu, having brought peace to all under Heaven through his campaigns, have had work to undertake!

At the moment when the four quarters were united, he divined a site and established his residence. These were matters whose circumstances scarcely allowed delay: establishing the state and securing its ruling house began here. Once the myriad people submitted gladly, he honored instruction and clarified righteousness. These were timely opportunities that could not simply be allowed to pass [?]: in founding his enterprise and transmitting his dynastic succession, he wished to make them sustainable by his successors. Thus, when the succession passed first to his son and then to his grandson, those who inherited his position and preserved his accomplishments would necessarily have an enduring foundation. By occupying an upstream position and setting the standard for all under Heaven, he would enable them to preserve it without loss; Heaven’s allotted succession would thereby secure [?] a foundation unshakable for a thousand years. Protecting the state and establishing orderly government, he laid down a lasting plan. Such measures as establishing the Biyong, the royal academy, to win the hearts of all under Heaven were intended to perpetuate this achievement without allowing it to lapse. Thus the sage’s great treasure, the throne, would foster boundless blessings for ten thousand years.

He planned for his descendants and bequeathed those plans to them; would the children whom he sheltered then enjoy security? Such were King Wu’s undertakings. Could this fail to count as being capable of ruling? For the way of rulership takes the bequest of peace to all under Heaven as …

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
貴匪一身一家已也今也丕烈佑啓後人而遠
圖有道於天下是曰作之元后者可徵矣人君
以天下長治爲難匪一時一事爾耳今也大統
克昌厥後而永置天下於無虞所謂垂拱而治
者在是矣豈不信乎其克君也哉夫以武王遷
都垂裕而慮天下也遠眞大聖人之所作爲也
周祚過曆其有自乎抑論武王天下之大聖也
以天下懷永圖天下之大業也然豈徒業而已
取殘伐罪始發於仁繼志述事終成乎孝仁孝
===
天子之大道也道在而業舉自隆矣而又何莫
不在學乎蓋當其時丹書之戒受之太公洪範
之疇聽之箕子其有得於學者深矣茲所以克
承帝王道統之傳而雖後世英君誼辟亦莫之
及也孟子曰武王不泄邇不忘遠其有見也夫
武丁孫子武王靡不勝龍旂十乘大糦是
承
陳治典
同考試官教諭袁　批〔武王靡不勝作者拘于〕
punctuated:
貴，匪一身一家已也。今也丕烈佑啓後人，而遠圖有道於天下，是曰作之元后者可徵矣。人君以天下長治爲難，匪一時一事爾耳。今也大統克昌厥後，而永置天下於無虞，所謂垂拱而治者在是矣。豈不信乎其克君也哉！夫以武王遷都垂裕，而慮天下也遠，眞大聖人之所作爲也。周祚過曆，其有自乎！抑論武王，天下之大聖也；以天下懷永圖，天下之大業也。然豈徒業而已？取殘伐罪，始發於仁；繼志述事，終成乎孝。仁孝，天子之大道也。道在而業舉自隆矣，而又何莫不在學乎？蓋當其時，丹書之戒受之太公，洪範之疇聽之箕子，其有得於學者深矣。茲所以克承帝王道統之傳，而雖後世英君誼辟亦莫之及也。孟子曰：「武王不泄邇，不忘遠。」其有見也夫！
武丁孫子，武王靡不勝。龍旂十乘，大糦是承。
陳治典
同考試官教諭袁　批〔武王靡不勝，作者拘于〕
translation_en:
…is what is valued, rather than merely the interests of one person or one family. Now his great achievements sustain and open the way for his successors, and his far-reaching plans accord with the Way in governing all under Heaven. Here we may find confirmation of what it means to become their sovereign. For a ruler, the difficulty lies in securing lasting order throughout the realm, rather than merely attending to a single occasion or affair. Now the great imperial succession flourishes among his descendants, and he establishes the realm forever free from anxiety. Here is what is meant by governing with robes hanging down and hands folded. Does this not indeed prove his ability to be a ruler? King Wu moved the capital and bequeathed prosperity, thinking far ahead for the realm: these were truly the deeds of a great sage. Surely there was a reason why the Zhou dynasty endured beyond its allotted span!
To consider King Wu further: he was a great sage of the world, and to devise enduring plans for all under Heaven was a great undertaking for the world. Yet was it merely an undertaking? Subduing the cruel and chastising the guilty began in benevolence; carrying forward his predecessor’s aspirations and completing his work culminated in filial devotion. Benevolence and filial devotion constitute the great Way of the Son of Heaven. Where the Way is present, his achievements naturally flourish in their entirety. And how could any of this fail to rest upon learning? In his time, he received the admonitions of the Cinnabar Writing from Taigong and heard the categories of the Great Plan explained by Jizi. What he gained through learning was profound. This was why he could inherit the transmission of the Way from the ancient emperors and kings, and why even the outstanding rulers and righteous sovereigns of later ages could not match him. Mencius said: “King Wu did not slight those near him, nor forget those far away.” Surely this was an insightful observation!
“The descendants of Wu Ding—the martial kings—were victorious in every endeavor. Ten chariots bearing dragon banners present the great millet offering.”
Chen Zhidian
Comment by Associate Examiner Yuan, Instructor: 〔On “the martial kings were victorious in every endeavor,” the writer confines himself to …〕

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
征伐此篇王政該舉且詞氣壯健真足以發明
賢王中興之盛
同考試官教諭王　批　大得天下心以崇典祀
正見商王克肖祖武此作得之而通篇詞意
正雅飭渾type登歌體義宜冠多士
同考試官教諭陳　批　莊重渾慤宛然商人口
氣
考試官教諭文　批　祖孫世德數言殆盡
考試官學正王　批　詞不煩而有餘味是作
頌者
===
商之嗣王剛德優於天下而得人祀乎其先也
蓋天下歸心王業之盛也商王肖有剛德而得
人以祀謂非遺休之有在哉此商人祭祀宗廟
之樂而至此言嗣王之蒙福也蓋曰繼世之君
莫貴於求世德而王者之福尤莫貴於大王業
也武丁孫子夫有所受之於先后矣而其承藉
之在今日者何如哉蓋聖武布昭祖德于今為
烈武王肖德襲號視昔有光中興圖治復舊物
punctuated:
征伐，此篇王政該舉，且詞氣壯健，真足以發明賢王中興之盛。
同考試官教諭王批：大得天下心，以崇典祀，正見商王克肖祖武。此作得之，而通篇詞意正雅飭渾type登歌體義，宜冠多士。
同考試官教諭陳批：莊重渾慤，宛然商人口氣。
考試官教諭文批：祖孫世德，數言殆盡。
考試官學正王批：詞不煩而有餘味，是作頌者。
商之嗣王，剛德優於天下，而得人祀乎其先也。蓋天下歸心，王業之盛也。商王肖有剛德，而得人以祀，謂非遺休之有在哉？此商人祭祀宗廟之樂，而至此言嗣王之蒙福也。蓋曰：繼世之君，莫貴於求世德，而王者之福，尤莫貴於大王業也。武丁孫子，夫有所受之於先后矣，而其承藉之在今日者何如哉？蓋聖武布昭，祖德于今為烈；武王肖德襲號，視昔有光。中興圖治，復舊物
translation_en:
…military campaigns. This essay encompasses kingly government in all its aspects; moreover, its language and spirit are vigorous, truly sufficient to illuminate the flourishing restoration achieved by a worthy king.
Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: By winning the allegiance of all under Heaven and thereby exalting the prescribed sacrifices, the Shang king demonstrated his ability to emulate his ancestors’ achievements. This composition captures that meaning. Throughout, its language and ideas are correct, elegant, disciplined, and rounded [?]; in the form and meaning appropriate to a hymn sung in the hall, it deserves first place among the candidates.
Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor, comments: Dignified, rounded, and sincere: unmistakably the voice of a man of Shang.
Examiner Wen, Instructor, comments: In a few words, it conveys almost exhaustively the virtue transmitted through generations from ancestor to descendant.
Examiner Wang, School Director, comments: Its language is economical yet leaves a lingering resonance. Here is someone who can compose a hymn of praise.
The successor king of Shang surpassed all under Heaven in firm virtue and secured men to offer sacrifices to his ancestors. For the allegiance of all under Heaven marks the flourishing of the royal enterprise. The Shang king inherited such firm virtue [?] and secured men to perform the sacrifices: could one say that the blessings bequeathed by his ancestors had no enduring presence? This is music used by the people of Shang in sacrifices at the ancestral temple; at this point it speaks of the blessings received by the successor king. Its meaning is this: for a ruler inheriting the throne, nothing is more precious than pursuing the virtue handed down through the generations; and among a king’s blessings, none is more precious than enlarging the royal enterprise. As a descendant of Wu Ding, he had indeed received something from the former sovereigns. But how did he sustain and draw upon that inheritance in his own day? Sagely martial prowess shone far and wide, and ancestral virtue was now manifested in glorious achievements. The martial king emulated that virtue and inherited that designation, adding luster to the past. He brought about a restoration, sought good government, and recovered the former patrimony…

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
然維新而一日萬幾憲天也勤民也不勞而理
凡以朝諸侯而有天下者猶運之掌也嘉靖戊
戌總乾綱以獨斷而九重百度禮樂也征伐也
舉之裕如所以平荊楚而服諸侯者綽有餘力
也是蓋視天下無難事而豈以不勝爲患夫懋
昭大烈有是不世出之君則下應僕志自無不
奉職之臣由是福貞既長合百官以承式宗廟
之祭得萬國之懽心建彼龍旂儼驂騑於十乘
諸侯之來亦衆矣則皆穆穡匪懈而王祭是供
===
焉秉溫恭虔執事敢違越乎烝嘗之期者無有
也承是大糦萃獻享於一堂相厥肆祀惟謹爾
敢曰黍稷非馨而明信弗將乎載清酤進和羹
駿奔走於對越之時者秩如也觀是諸侯之畢
歸而方命厥后同休矣是則君德之隆人心之
所由歸也王業之所由盛也而天命之所由固
不外是矣嗣王享治有此茲非先后之福之所
遺乎噫此商人宗廟登歌不敢忘所自也考之
天造商室由湯至於武丁天下歸殷久矣然聖
punctuated: 然維新，而一日萬幾，憲天也，勤民也，不勞而理。凡以朝諸侯而有天下者，猶運之掌也。嘉靖戊戌，總乾綱以獨斷，而九重百度，禮樂也，征伐也，舉之裕如。所以平荊楚而服諸侯者，綽有餘力也。是蓋視天下無難事，而豈以不勝爲患？夫懋昭大烈，有是不世出之君，則下應僕志，自無不奉職之臣。由是福貞既長，合百官以承式，宗廟之祭，得萬國之懽心。建彼龍旂，儼驂騑於十乘，諸侯之來亦衆矣。則皆穆穡匪懈，而王祭是供焉。秉溫恭，虔執事，敢違越乎烝嘗之期者，無有也。承是大糦，萃獻享於一堂，相厥肆祀惟謹爾。敢曰黍稷非馨，而明信弗將乎？載清酤，進和羹，駿奔走於對越之時者，秩如也。觀是諸侯之畢歸，而方命厥后同休矣。是則君德之隆，人心之所由歸也，王業之所由盛也，而天命之所由固，不外是矣。嗣王享治有此，茲非先后之福之所遺乎？噫！此商人宗廟登歌，不敢忘所自也。考之天造商室，由湯至於武丁，天下歸殷久矣。然聖
translation_en:
…yet bringing renewal. Amid the myriad affairs of each day, he modeled himself on Heaven and labored for the people, bringing order without strain. To receive the feudal lords at court and possess all under Heaven was as easy as turning something in his palm. In the wuxu year of Jiajing [1538], he gathered the sovereign authority into his own hands and decided affairs alone. The hundred institutions of the innermost court—rites and music, military expeditions and punitive campaigns—he managed with ease. He therefore had strength to spare in pacifying Jing and Chu and bringing the feudal lords into submission. To him, it seems, nothing under Heaven was difficult; how could he have worried that his powers were insufficient?

He splendidly manifested his great achievements. With such a ruler, who appears but rarely in the ages, those below answered the servant’s purpose [?], and naturally no minister failed to discharge his duties. Thus his enduring blessings increased [?], and all officials joined in upholding the established forms. The sacrifices in the ancestral temple won the joyful allegiance of the myriad states. Dragon banners were raised, and the outer horses stood in solemn array beside ten chariots: numerous indeed were the feudal lords who came. All were reverent and diligent in agriculture [?], supplying the royal sacrifices. Maintaining gentleness and reverence, they performed their duties devoutly; none dared disregard the appointed times of the winter and autumn sacrifices. They presented these great sacrificial offerings, gathering their gifts in a single hall, and assisted with the rites in utmost care. Could they dare say that millet’s fragrance was not what mattered, and therefore fail to present manifest sincerity? They brought clear wine and offered harmoniously seasoned broth. Those who hastened about in attendance before the spirits did so in orderly ranks.

Observe how all the feudal lords gave their allegiance and shared their ruler’s blessings [?]. It was the greatness of the ruler’s virtue that drew people’s hearts to him, made the royal enterprise flourish, and secured Heaven’s mandate: none of these arose from anything beyond this. When the succeeding king enjoyed such good government, was this not a blessing bequeathed by the former kings? Ah! This is why the people of Shang, in the hymns sung in their ancestral temple, dared not forget the source of their blessings. Considering how Heaven established the house of Shang, from Tang down to Wuding, all under Heaven had long given allegiance to Yin. Yet the sage…

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
徹日躋恭默思道則固湯與高宗治天下之大
本也而後人祀之必曰武云者豈其不足於文
耶蓋順天應人匪武不克中興復古武莫先焉
而文德固未嘗不運行乎其中也故王以七十
里者必始於十一征而無敵而三年之克始可
以建四方之極耳否則殆而已矣語曰君德以
剛為主斯則有天下者所當念
春秋
秦人伐晉〔文公三年〕晉侯伐秦〔文公四年〕狄公
伐邾〔八月己酉〕入邾以邾子益來〔哀公七年〕
歸邾子益于邾〔哀公八年〕
===
同考試官教諭甘　批　秦穆魯哀之事孔子備
存而弗削者以穆能改過哀知去惡也場中作
者漫無所見聖人書法隱矣此篇微顯闡幽渾
融傳意而輕重有準如老吏斷獄森然不亂也
考試官教諭文　批　四傳兩意體認精當而
又渾淪無迹傑作也
孫元卿
punctuated:
徹日躋，恭默思道，則固湯與高宗治天下之大本也。而後人祀之，必曰武云者，豈其不足於文耶？蓋順天應人，匪武不克；中興復古，武莫先焉。而文德固未嘗不運行乎其中也。故王以七十里者，必始於十一征而無敵；而三年之克，始可以建四方之極耳。否則殆而已矣。語曰：「君德以剛為主。」斯則有天下者所當念。

春秋

秦人伐晉〔文公三年〕。晉侯伐秦〔文公四年〕。狄公伐邾〔八月己酉〕，入邾，以邾子益來〔哀公七年〕。歸邾子益于邾〔哀公八年〕。

同考試官教諭甘批：秦穆、魯哀之事，孔子備存而弗削者，以穆能改過，哀知去惡也。場中作者漫無所見，聖人書法隱矣。此篇微顯闡幽，渾融傳意，而輕重有準，如老吏斷獄，森然不亂也。

考試官教諭文批：四傳兩意，體認精當，而又渾淪無迹，傑作也。

孫元卿
translation_en:
…penetrating understanding and daily advancement, reverent silence and contemplation of the Way: these were indeed the great foundations upon which Tang and Gaozong governed the world. Yet when later generations sacrificed to them, they invariably spoke of their martial prowess. Could this mean that they were deficient in civil virtue? To accord with Heaven and respond to the people could not be accomplished without martial prowess; in restoring a dynasty and reviving antiquity, nothing took precedence over it. Yet civil virtue was always at work within these undertakings. Thus, he who rose to kingship from a territory of seventy li first had to undertake eleven campaigns and prove invincible; only after the conquest achieved in three years could the other establish the highest standard for the four quarters. Otherwise, there would have been nothing but peril. As the saying goes, “The ruler’s virtue rests principally on firmness.” This is something that those who possess All-under-Heaven should bear in mind.

Spring and Autumn Annals

The men of Qin attacked Jin. 〔Third year of Duke Wen.〕 The lord of Jin attacked Qin. 〔Fourth year of Duke Wen.〕 Duke Di [?] attacked Zhu 〔On the jiyou day of the eighth month〕, entered Zhu, and brought back Yi, Viscount of Zhu. 〔Seventh year of Duke Ai.〕 Yi, Viscount of Zhu, was returned to Zhu. 〔Eighth year of Duke Ai.〕

Comment by Associate Examiner Gan, Instructor: Confucius preserved the affairs of Duke Mu of Qin and Duke Ai of Lu in full, without excising them, because Mu could correct his faults and Ai knew to abandon wrongdoing. The candidates in the examination hall generally failed to perceive this, leaving the sage’s principles of recording events obscure. This essay brings subtle meanings to light and elucidates what is hidden. It thoroughly integrates the meanings of the commentaries while assigning due weight to each point, like an experienced official deciding legal cases: rigorous and orderly throughout.

Comment by Examiner Wen, Instructor: The four commentaries and their two underlying meanings are understood with precision and aptness, and are seamlessly integrated without any trace of effort. A masterpiece.

Sun Yuanqing

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
考試官學正王　批　得謹嚴筆法
強國貳過而能改春秋深善之望國稔惡而能
夫春秋特美之此秦晉脩怨致嚴於人爵之間
魯哀虐邾無侯乎婉以成章也春秋其王道之
權衡也歟何則易曰君子懲忿窒慾乃知脩德
者非過之患而能改之貴也春秋諸侯知改者
鮮矣何幸於秦穆見之蓋秦晉世讐也晉無望
焉術矣秦自殽函而誓詞作似也復決楚舟而
後快其於悔過之誠爲何如君子曰穆也猶夫
===
人而已矣孰意深懲既往大冀將來見伐不報
會憤之兵遂息焉則是佳兵之戒有以得遠怨
之方質之自誓之言始踐矣良士之思其尚有
蹇叔矣乎噫穆可謂不遠而復者矣其視專尚
威力者賢不肖何如耶經之人秦爵晉君子有
以辯之不然秦誓何取也安能序書與典謨篇
並列耶易曰君子遷善改過乃知進德者非惡
之患而務去之難也春秋諸侯知去者鮮矣何
幸於魯哀見之蓋邾魯隣壤也邾當畦焉者矣
punctuated:
考試官學正王　批：得謹嚴筆法。

強國貳過而能改，春秋深善之；望國稔惡而能夫，春秋特美之。此秦晉脩怨，致嚴於人爵之間；魯哀虐邾，無侯乎？婉以成章也。春秋其王道之權衡也歟！何則？易曰：「君子懲忿窒慾。」乃知脩德者非過之患，而能改之貴也。春秋諸侯知改者鮮矣，何幸於秦穆見之！蓋秦晉世讐也，晉無望焉術矣。秦自殽函而誓詞作，似也；復決楚舟而後快，其於悔過之誠爲何如？君子曰：「穆也猶夫人而已矣。」孰意深懲既往，大冀將來，見伐不報，會憤之兵遂息焉。則是佳兵之戒，有以得遠怨之方；質之自誓之言，始踐矣。良士之思，其尚有蹇叔矣乎？噫！穆可謂不遠而復者矣。其視專尚威力者，賢不肖何如耶？經之人秦爵晉，君子有以辯之。不然，秦誓何取也？安能序書，與典謨篇並列耶？易曰：「君子遷善改過。」乃知進德者非惡之患，而務去之難也。春秋諸侯知去者鮮矣，何幸於魯哀見之！蓋邾魯隣壤也，邾當畦焉者矣。
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Wang, an Instructor: “It achieves a precise and rigorous manner of expression.”

When a powerful state repeats a fault but can reform, the Spring and Autumn Annals deeply approves it; when an eminent state persists in wrongdoing but can [remove it?], the Spring and Autumn Annals especially praises it. Thus, in recording Qin and Jin’s pursuit of their feud, it exercises strict judgment through the distinction between calling their rulers “men” and according them noble rank. When Duke Ai of Lu maltreated Zhu, was he not denied the designation “marquis”? Its meaning takes shape through subtle wording. Are the Spring and Autumn Annals not the scales by which the Kingly Way is weighed?

Why is this so? The Book of Changes says: “The gentleman restrains anger and checks desire.” We thus know that, for one cultivating virtue, the concern is not having faults; what is precious is being able to correct them. Among the feudal lords of the Spring and Autumn period, few knew how to reform. How fortunate that we see this in Duke Mu of Qin! Qin and Jin were hereditary enemies; nothing could be hoped for from Jin [?]. After the events at Yao and Han, Qin produced the words of an oath: this seemed fitting. Yet he again destroyed the boats of Chu [?] before feeling satisfied. What does this say about the sincerity of his repentance? The gentleman says: “Mu was merely an ordinary man.”

Who would have expected him profoundly to take warning from the past and place great hopes in the future? Attacked, he did not retaliate, and the warfare born of accumulated anger [?] consequently ceased. Thus, by heeding the warning against delighting in arms, he found a means of keeping resentment at a distance. Measured against the words of his own oath, he had at last begun to fulfill them. In his longing for worthy men, did he still have Jian Shu in mind? Ah! Mu may be called one who returned before straying far. Compared with those who prize force alone, how do their respective worth and unworthiness stand? The gentleman can explain why the Classic calls Qin’s ruler a “man” while according Jin’s ruler his noble title. Otherwise, what merit would there be in the “Oath of Qin”? How could it be placed in the Book of Documents alongside the Canons and Counsels?

The Book of Changes says: “The gentleman moves toward goodness and corrects his faults.” We thus know that, for one advancing in virtue, the concern is not wrongdoing itself; the difficulty lies in striving to remove it. Among the feudal lords of the Spring and Autumn period, few knew how to remove wrongdoing. How fortunate that we see this in Duke Ai of Lu! Zhu and Lu shared a border, and Zhu was situated at its boundary [?]…

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
魯從季孟而范門入過矣況辱負瑕以相殘其
於字小之仁爲何如君子曰哀也天下之惡莫
大矣所幸困衡於人悔悟於己乃反其君社稷
之奉有常焉則是反正之善足以盖前行之愆
貿之怙終之刑可免矣侵疆以歸其始乎景偪
也哉噫哀可謂困而反則者矣其視長惡不悛
者得與失何如耶經之備始錄終君子有以辯
之不然春秋魯史也安能直書與獻舞事例論
耶是則秦穆惟深與也而後克己之功著魯哀
===
惟弗諱也而後自新之路開其聖人樂與人爲
善之心歟抑穆哀可同語耶秦誓一篇既列於
書曾子復述於大學穆其與聖賢伍矣哀卒削
弱不競適越之辱不免焉二公非其匹也明矣
噫敝然後而霸業成用孟明也而況不爲孟明
者乎有其儒而弗究其用哀可惜哉
春王正月公及齊侯平莒及郯莒人不肯
公伐莒取向〔宣公四年〕
洪遇
punctuated:
魯從季孟而范門入，過矣。況辱負瑕以相殘，其於字小之仁爲何如？君子曰：「哀也，天下之惡莫大矣。」所幸困衡於人，悔悟於己，乃反其君，社稷之奉有常焉。則是反正之善，足以盖前行之愆，貿之怙終之刑可免矣。侵疆以歸，其始乎？景偪也哉？噫！哀可謂困而反則者矣。其視長惡不悛者，得與失何如耶？經之備始錄終，君子有以辯之。不然，《春秋》，魯史也，安能直書，與獻舞事例論耶？是則秦穆惟深與也，而後克己之功著；魯哀惟弗諱也，而後自新之路開。其聖人樂與人爲善之心歟？抑穆、哀可同語耶？《秦誓》一篇既列於《書》，曾子復述於《大學》，穆其與聖賢伍矣。哀卒削弱不競，適越之辱不免焉。二公非其匹也，明矣。噫！敝然後而霸業成，用孟明也，而況不爲孟明者乎？有其儒而弗究其用，哀可惜哉！
春王正月，公及齊侯平莒及郯，莒人不肯。公伐莒，取向。〔宣公四年〕
洪遇
translation_en:
…Lu followed the Ji and Meng clans and entered through the Fan Gate: this was a transgression. Moreover, it inflicted the humiliation at Fuxia, doing further harm. How did this accord with the benevolence of nurturing smaller states? The gentleman says: “As for Duke Ai, no evil under Heaven was greater.” Fortunately, constrained and thwarted by others, he came to remorse and understanding within himself. He then returned their ruler, and regular sacrifices at their altars of soil and grain were assured. Thus, the goodness of his return to what was right sufficed to cover his earlier faults, and the punishment for persisting in wrongdoing could be avoided [?]. Was returning the territory he had invaded the beginning of this? Was it because Jing pressed him [?]? Ah! Ai may be called one who returned to the proper rule after encountering adversity. Compared with those who perpetuate evil without repenting, how do his gains and losses stand? The gentleman can discern why the Classic fully recounts the beginning and records the outcome. Otherwise, since the Spring and Autumn Annals is Lu’s own history, how could it record the matter frankly and allow it to be discussed alongside the case of Xianwu?
Thus, only through the profound approval accorded Duke Mu of Qin did his achievement in mastering himself become manifest; only through the refusal to conceal Duke Ai of Lu’s faults was the path to his renewal opened. Does this express the sage’s readiness to help others do good? Yet can Mu and Ai be spoken of on equal terms? The “Oath of Qin” was included in the Book of Documents, and Master Zeng cited it again in the Great Learning: Mu thereby joined the company of sages and worthies. Ai, however, ultimately became weakened and powerless, and could not escape the humiliation of going to Yue. Clearly, the two dukes were not equals. Ah! That he established his hegemony after defeat was because he employed Mengming. How much more could have been achieved with someone greater than Mengming! Ai had his Confucian scholar, yet failed to make full use of him. How regrettable!
In spring, in the first month of the royal calendar, the duke and the Marquis of Qi made peace between Ju and Tan. The people of Ju refused to accept it. The duke attacked Ju and took Xiang. 〔Fourth year of Duke Xuan〕
Hong Yu.

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭卄　批　魯宣私鄭失平怨之道
故竟至伐莒取向經旨自明作者多泥伐取遂
致輕重無別獨此篇得之而詞氣嚴正使宣公
有聞自當汗顏愳怩
考試官教諭文　批　順快峻整
考試官學正王　批　有法度有筆力
春秋譏望國平人之怨起於意而成於我也蓋
事貴無容心焉爾矣魯宣平莒郯以私始以亂
終之其斯見譏於春秋也與且魯何爲而平莒
===
及郯也郯莒讐也何爲而伐莒取向也莒弗從
也然則可乎蓋天下之感惟正斯應天下之情
惟公乃服故凡物不得其平則鳴而君子行有
不得反諸已魯欲平莒及郯也苟能直以開其
意虛以待其來持鑑空衡平之心爲解紛釋怨
之地則信可孚於言前誠自昭於令外而郯莒
將自釋矣柰何郯私𥬇也比之以爲朋齊大國
也挾之以爲重自以強弱莫予違而曲直非彼
由也抑不知莫強於人心而同然之喻不容於
punctuated:
同考試官教諭卄批：魯宣私鄭，失平怨之道，故竟至伐莒取向。經旨自明，作者多泥伐取，遂致輕重無別。獨此篇得之，而詞氣嚴正，使宣公有聞，自當汗顏愳怩。
考試官教諭文批：順快峻整。
考試官學正王批：有法度，有筆力。
《春秋》譏望國平人之怨，起於意而成於我也。蓋事貴無容心焉爾矣。魯宣平莒郯，以私始，以亂終之，其斯見譏於《春秋》也與！且魯何爲而平莒及郯也？郯莒讐也。何爲而伐莒取向也？莒弗從也。然則可乎？蓋天下之感，惟正斯應；天下之情，惟公乃服。故凡物不得其平則鳴，而君子行有不得，反諸已。魯欲平莒及郯也，苟能直以開其意，虛以待其來，持鑑空衡平之心，爲解紛釋怨之地，則信可孚於言前，誠自昭於令外，而郯莒將自釋矣。柰何郯私𥬇也，比之以爲朋；齊大國也，挾之以爲重。自以強弱莫予違，而曲直非彼由也。抑不知莫強於人心，而同然之喻不容於
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Nian [?], Instructor: Duke Xuan of Lu favored Zheng [?], losing sight of the proper way to reconcile grievances, and thus ultimately attacked Ju and seized Xiang. The meaning of the Classic is clear in itself. Most writers become fixated on the attack and seizure, thereby failing to distinguish the relative importance of the issues. This essay alone grasps the point, and its language and tone are stern and upright. Were Duke Xuan to hear it, he would surely blush with shame and embarrassment [?].
Comment by Examiner Wen, Instructor: Fluent and incisive, rigorous and orderly.
Comment by Examiner Wang, Instructor: It has disciplined composition and forceful writing.
The Spring and Autumn Annals censures a leading state for settling others’ grievances when the undertaking springs from its own intentions and is carried through according to its own will. In handling affairs, what matters is simply to admit no private motives. Duke Xuan of Lu’s reconciliation of Ju and Tan began with partiality and ended in disorder. Was this not why he was censured in the Spring and Autumn Annals? Why, then, did Lu seek to reconcile Ju and Tan? Because Tan and Ju were enemies. Why did it attack Ju and seize Xiang? Because Ju would not comply. But was this permissible?
For among all under Heaven, only uprightness elicits a response, and only impartiality wins people’s willing submission. Thus anything denied equitable treatment cries out; and when the gentleman’s actions fail to achieve their purpose, he turns back to examine himself. In seeking to reconcile Ju and Tan, if Lu could have opened their minds through uprightness, received their approaches without preconceptions, and maintained a mind like an unclouded mirror and an even balance, providing common ground for resolving disputes and dispelling grievances, then its trustworthiness could have inspired confidence before any words were spoken, and its sincerity would have shone forth beyond its commands. Tan and Ju would then have relinquished their grievances of their own accord.
Why instead treat Tan as a private associate [?], drawing close to it as an ally, and rely on Qi, a great state, to lend weight to one’s position? Lu supposed that, strong or weak, none would defy it, and that right and wrong were not for the others to determine. Yet it did not understand that nothing is stronger than the human heart, and that the understanding shared by all cannot admit of …

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
言強莫柔於人心而服義之機不可以力屈是
故偏係之私不足以輸其款而威力之搏適有
以激其忿艴然不悅揖而去之固其所也顧乃
拂逆順之情不知反諸己情強大之力徒欲責
之人加之以師聲其罪也將何以爲詞奪其所
有刼以威也人其謂我何不顧其理徒以無道
行之謂之強可也盡言以相正寧不愧於心乎
不揆其分狡焉思以啓之謂之盜可也正法以
相求不亦在所損乎名曰息爭非不善也不以
===
禮而以勢是以亂易亂耳詩謂不忮不求公其
昧之名曰善隣非不美也不以義而以利是以
燕伐燕耳傳謂反仁反智公何有焉經故書及
見其所欲書取名之爲盜乎者魯之意不肯者
莒之心也公之失豈能掩哉大抵聖人感人心
而天下和平誠信孚也故邾射不貴盟誓而獨
取必於區區一子路豈非誠信素孚而自不能
違耶宣以千乘而顧不能行於一莒也噫人之
生也直宣其枉也已雖然過市之哀將不容於
punctuated: 言強；莫柔於人心，而服義之機不可以力屈。是故偏係之私不足以輸其款，而威力之搏適有以激其忿。艴然不悅，揖而去之，固其所也。顧乃拂逆順之情，不知反諸己；情強大之力，徒欲責之人。加之以師，聲其罪也，將何以爲詞？奪其所有，刼以威也，人其謂我何？不顧其理，徒以無道行之，謂之強可也；盡言以相正，寧不愧於心乎？不揆其分，狡焉思以啓之，謂之盜可也；正法以相求，不亦在所損乎？名曰息爭，非不善也；不以禮而以勢，是以亂易亂耳。《詩》謂「不忮不求」，公其昧之。名曰善隣，非不美也；不以義而以利，是以燕伐燕耳。《傳》謂「反仁反智」，公何有焉？《經》故書「及」，見其所欲；書「取」，名之爲盜。「乎」者，魯之意；「不肯」者，莒之心也。公之失，豈能掩哉？大抵聖人感人心而天下和平，誠信孚也。故邾射不貴盟誓，而獨取必於區區一子路，豈非誠信素孚而自不能違耶？宣以千乘，而顧不能行於一莒也。噫！人之生也直，宣其枉也已！雖然，過市之哀將不容於
translation_en:
…to be coerced by words. Nothing is more yielding than the human heart, yet its impulse to submit to righteousness cannot be compelled by force. Thus, the selfishness of partisan attachment cannot convey sincerity, while the assault of coercive power only provokes resentment. That they should grow angry and displeased, bow, and depart was only natural. Yet the duke disregarded their feelings about what was right and wrong and failed to examine himself. Relying on his superior power [?], he sought only to blame others. If he attacked them with an army and proclaimed their guilt, what grounds could he give? If he seized their possessions and intimidated them with force, what would people say of him? To disregard principle and act without the Way could properly be called coercion. If they spoke fully and frankly to correct one another, would he not feel shame in his heart? To disregard the limits of his rightful position and craftily seek to expand his territory could properly be called robbery. If they held one another to the proper standards of law, would he not suffer loss?

In name, ending strife was certainly good; but to employ power instead of ritual propriety was merely to replace one disorder with another. The Book of Odes says, “Neither malicious nor grasping”; the duke seems to have been blind to this. In name, maintaining good relations with neighbors was certainly admirable; but to act for profit instead of righteousness was merely to use Yan to attack Yan. The commentary says to “examine one’s own benevolence and examine one’s own wisdom.” What trace of these did the duke possess? Thus the Classic writes “joined with,” revealing what he desired, and writes “took,” designating his action as robbery. “Peace” [?] expressed Lu’s intention; “would not consent” expressed the feelings of Ju. How could the duke’s failure be concealed?

In general, when the sage moves people’s hearts and all under Heaven becomes peaceful and harmonious, it is because sincerity and trustworthiness win their confidence. Thus Zhu She [?] placed no value on covenants and oaths, but sought assurance solely from the single person of Zilu. Was this not because Zilu’s sincerity and trustworthiness had long inspired confidence, so that Zhu She could not bring himself to go against him? Yet Duke Xuan, with a thousand chariots, could not make his will prevail even in Ju alone. Alas! People live by uprightness; how crooked Duke Xuan was! Nevertheless, the grief of passing through the marketplace would find no place within…

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
天地間會之怨誰其平之宜之狂也久矣
禮記
在朝言禮問禮對以禮
殷士儋
同考試官教諭魏　批〔此題字少義多難于體〕
認析理精當而詞氣簡古僅見此作
考試官教諭文　批〔句句皆禮無一漫語〕
考試官學正王　批〔完全縝密不見其難〕
人臣之立朝言必稽於禮也夫禮之為物大矣
===
朝言而弗之及豈所以為言乎記曲禮者謂夫
禮無乎不在而言必有所當是故在官言官在
府言府在庫言庫明各有司也其在朝也則何
以哉蓋人君臨御之地道德仁義於是乎成焉
教訓正俗於是乎表焉不惟禮之道也則品節
之未備何以為揆道範物之方是故言之不可
以已矣百官表著之所朝宗覲遇於是乎會焉
燕饗慶賜於是乎行焉苟舍禮而言也則度數
之弗閑何以為序事詔相之則是故語必在所
punctuated:
天地間，會之怨誰其平之？宜之狂也久矣。

《禮記》
在朝言禮，問禮，對以禮。
殷士儋

同考試官教諭魏批〔此題字少義多，難于體〕認析理精當，而詞氣簡古，僅見此作。
考試官教諭文批〔句句皆禮，無一漫語〕
考試官學正王批〔完全縝密，不見其難〕

人臣之立朝，言必稽於禮也。夫禮之為物大矣，朝言而弗之及，豈所以為言乎？記《曲禮》者謂夫禮無乎不在，而言必有所當。是故在官言官，在府言府，在庫言庫，明各有司也。其在朝也，則何以哉？蓋人君臨御之地，道德仁義於是乎成焉，教訓正俗於是乎表焉。不惟禮之道也，則品節之未備，何以為揆道範物之方？是故言之不可以已矣。百官表著之所，朝宗覲遇於是乎會焉，燕饗慶賜於是乎行焉。苟舍禮而言也，則度數之弗閑，何以為序事詔相之則？是故語必在所
translation_en:
…between Heaven and Earth. Who, then, will redress Hui’s resentment [?]? Yi’s madness has persisted for a long time [?].

Record of Rites
“In court, speak of ritual; ask about ritual; answer in accordance with ritual.”
Yin Shidan

Comment by Associate Examiner Wei, Instructor: “This topic has few words but many meanings and is difficult to comprehend. The analysis of principle is precise and apt, while the diction and tone are concise and antique. This is the only essay of its kind I have seen.” [The annotation boundary interrupts “comprehend” in the transcription.]
Comment by Examiner Wen, Instructor: “Every sentence concerns ritual; not a single remark is irrelevant.”
Comment by Examiner Wang, School Instructor: “Complete and meticulous, it gives no sign of the difficulty involved.”

When a minister takes his place at court, his speech must accord with ritual. Ritual is indeed a vast matter. If speech at court does not touch upon it, how can such speech fulfill its purpose? The compiler of “Summary of the Rules of Propriety” explains that ritual is present everywhere, but that speech must suit its setting. Thus, in an office one speaks of official business; in a treasury, of treasury business; in a storehouse, of storehouse business. This makes clear that each has its own responsibilities. What, then, should one speak of at court?

The court is where the ruler presides. There the Way, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness are brought to fulfillment; there instruction and the rectification of customs are made manifest. If no thought is given to the way of ritual, its distinctions and regulations will remain incomplete: how could there then be a means of measuring conduct against the Way and setting standards for affairs? Thus, speaking of ritual cannot cease.

The court is also where the hundred officials occupy their prescribed stations. There the various audiences with the sovereign take place; there banquets, feasts, celebrations, and bestowals are conducted. If one abandons ritual in speaking, its measures and prescribed forms will remain unmastered: how could there then be rules for ordering affairs and guiding and assisting their conduct? Thus, speech must be grounded in…

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
稽矣如其有疑而問乎將何以定親疎將何以
決嫌疑本之天叙天秩之故而質其要領之所
歸不他及也其或因問而對乎如斯以別同異
如斯以明是非稽諸經禮曲禮之詳而語以節
文之異尚無贅詞也問以禮而對以禮本末必
昭焉則所以達天道而明人情者在是矣不然
以朝廷之大也而豈無可言者乎陳其數而必
知其義論辯必悉焉則所以辨上下而別等威
者在是矣不然非有守之士也而可以事君乎
===
於是見臣子立□□□何也有禮則安無
禮則危夫人以之而□□□故三歸之設八佾
之舞以至雍門之作郊牛之改卜要皆不講於
禮之過也入太廟而每事問在朝廷而便便惟
謹夫子豈徒也哉故曰聖人以禮示之故天下
國家可得而正也此立朝者之所當知也
樂也者聖人之所樂也而可以善民心其
感人深其移風易俗故先王著其教焉
宋鰲
punctuated:
稽矣。如其有疑而問乎，將何以定親疎，將何以決嫌疑？本之天叙天秩之故，而質其要領之所歸，不他及也。其或因問而對乎，如斯以別同異，如斯以明是非，稽諸經禮曲禮之詳，而語以節文之異，尚無贅詞也。問以禮而對以禮，本末必昭焉，則所以達天道而明人情者在是矣。不然，以朝廷之大也，而豈無可言者乎？陳其數而必知其義，論辯必悉焉，則所以辨上下而別等威者在是矣。不然，非有守之士也，而可以事君乎？於是見臣子立□□□，何也？有禮則安，無禮則危，夫人以之而□□□。故三歸之設、八佾之舞，以至雍門之作、郊牛之改卜，要皆不講於禮之過也。入太廟而每事問，在朝廷而便便惟謹，夫子豈徒也哉？故曰：「聖人以禮示之，故天下國家可得而正也。」此立朝者之所當知也。

樂也者，聖人之所樂也，而可以善民心。其感人深，其移風易俗，故先王著其教焉。

宋鰲。
translation_en:
…be examined. If one has doubts and asks questions, how is one to determine degrees of kinship, and how is one to resolve uncertainties? One grounds oneself in the principles of Heaven’s ordering of human relationships and ceremonial ranks, and examines where their essentials lead, without straying into other matters. If one answers a question, one thereby distinguishes sameness from difference and clarifies right and wrong. One consults the detailed provisions of fundamental rites and particular observances, and speaks of their differing forms and regulations, still without superfluous words. When questions and answers alike concern ritual, both foundations and particulars must become clear. Herein lies the means of comprehending Heaven’s Way and understanding human feelings. Otherwise, in so great a setting as the imperial court, could there be nothing worth discussing? In setting forth ritual prescriptions, one must understand their meaning; discussion and analysis must be exhaustive. Herein lies the means of distinguishing superior from inferior and differentiating the dignities of rank. Otherwise, how could someone without steadfast principles serve his ruler?

Here we see how a minister establishes himself [three characters illegible, ?]. Why is this? With ritual there is security; without ritual there is danger. People, through it, [three characters illegible, ?]. Thus the establishment of the Sangui, the performance of the eight-row dance, and even the making of the Yongmen [?] and the renewed divination concerning the ox for the suburban sacrifice were all, in essence, faults arising from failure to study ritual. Entering the Grand Ancestral Temple, the Master asked about every matter; at court, he spoke fluently yet with utmost care. Could his conduct have been without purpose? Thus it is said: “The sage shows them ritual; hence all under Heaven, the states, and the families can be set right.” This is what those who serve at court should understand.

Music is what the sages delight in, and it can make the people’s hearts good. It moves people deeply and transforms customs; therefore the former kings established instruction in it.

Song Ao.

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭魏　批　〔聖人之于樂也說諸心施諸政立其教由一心以及于無窮也此篇發〕
〔揮明盡而次第輕重令人灑然興起〕
考試官教諭文　批　〔有源委有血脉善言聖人之樂〕
考試官學正王　批　〔通篇皆樂不屑用時句慕古脫俗之士也〕
記者原聖人作樂以成化而因以廣教也夫生
民之道樂之所關者大也聖人樂和平而天下
應之立教自不容已矣古昔聖人之爲樂也固
===
以象至德之光而實以彰太和之化其道不亦
深乎是故鍾鼓管磬非極音也而欣喜歡愛之
情出矣羽籥干戚以飾貌也而優柔平中之德
宣焉樂非聖人之所樂矣乎由是舉而措之也
至和之運足以神感化之機非有所強也合愛
之流有以導民心於善孰得而違之其感於內
也君子以好善小人以聽過乎好惡而反人道
之正不徒革面已耳其成於習也君好而臣爲
punctuated:
同考試官教諭魏批〔聖人之于樂也，說諸心，施諸政，立其教，由一心以及于無窮也。此篇發揮明盡，而次第輕重，令人灑然興起。〕
考試官教諭文批〔有源委，有血脉，善言聖人之樂。〕
考試官學正王批〔通篇皆樂，不屑用時句，慕古脫俗之士也。〕
記者原聖人作樂以成化，而因以廣教也。夫生民之道，樂之所關者大也。聖人樂和平，而天下應之，立教自不容已矣。古昔聖人之爲樂也，固以象至德之光，而實以彰太和之化，其道不亦深乎？是故鍾鼓管磬，非極音也，而欣喜歡愛之情出矣；羽籥干戚，以飾貌也，而優柔平中之德宣焉。樂非聖人之所樂矣乎？由是舉而措之也，至和之運，足以神感化之機，非有所強也。合愛之流，有以導民心於善，孰得而違之？其感於內也，君子以好善，小人以聽，過乎好惡而反人道之正，不徒革面已耳。其成於習也，君好而臣爲
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Wei, Instructor, comments: 〔For the sage, music brings delight to the heart and finds application in government. In establishing its teaching, he extends what proceeds from a single heart without limit. This essay develops the subject clearly and fully; its ordering and distribution of emphasis refresh and inspire the reader.〕
Examiner Wen, Instructor, comments: 〔It traces both origins and ramifications and has an interconnected argument. It speaks well of the sage’s music.〕
Examiner Wang, Assistant Instructor, comments: 〔The entire essay concerns music. Disdaining fashionable turns of phrase, its author is a scholar who admires antiquity and rises above vulgar convention.〕
The author of the Record of Rites investigates how the sages created music to accomplish moral transformation and thereby extend their teaching. In the ordering of human life, music has profound consequences. The sage delights in peace and harmony, and all under Heaven respond to him; establishing this teaching is therefore something he cannot leave undone. When the sages of antiquity made music, they certainly intended to represent the radiance of consummate virtue, but also, in substance, to manifest the transforming influence of supreme harmony. Is its Way not profound?
Thus bells, drums, pipes, and chime stones do not merely bring sound to its fullest expression: through them emerge feelings of joy, delight, affection, and love. Feather plumes, flutes, shields, and axes embellish outward appearance, yet through them are expressed the virtues of gentleness, equanimity, and balance. Is music not what the sage delights in? When he puts it into practice, the operation of perfect harmony is sufficient to make the workings of moral transformation wondrously effective; there is no coercion. The current of mutual affection can guide the people’s hearts toward goodness: who could resist it?
In its inward influence, it leads the gentleman to love goodness and the common person to heed instruction; they transcend likes and dislikes [?] and return to the proper human Way. It does not merely change their outward appearance. As its effects become established through habitual practice, the ruler delights in it and his ministers undertake…

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
之上行而民從之回風俗而爲淳厚之歸有不
丕變者乎先王知夫樂之不可以已也是以本
之情性稽之度數而設教以示歸極之方廣其
節奏省其文采而立等以崇孫業之術德厚是
繩也而以達之萬方之大人心之感也殆無窮
矣事行侅象也而以昭諸後世之遠風俗之善
也不有未哉使聖人作樂以平天下之情而不
著之以爲教則其道或幾乎息矣將何以觀德
乎故曰樂者天地之命中和之紀人情之所不
===
能免者也獨樂其志而不厭其道備舉其道而
不私其欲則可以達於天下後世矣茍非身有
其德而求之聲容之末其能淑乎故兒寬曰惟
天子建中和之極蓋謂此也當時宣房瓠子之
作天馬寶鼎之歌亦有協於是否乎
第貳場
論
萬世不可易之定論
潘龍
punctuated:
之，上行而民從之，回風俗而爲淳厚之歸，有不丕變者乎？先王知夫樂之不可以已也，是以本之情性，稽之度數，而設教以示歸極之方；廣其節奏，省其文采，而立等以崇孫業之術。德厚是繩也，而以達之萬方之大，人心之感也，殆無窮矣。事行侅象也，而以昭諸後世之遠，風俗之善也，不有未哉？使聖人作樂以平天下之情，而不著之以爲教，則其道或幾乎息矣，將何以觀德乎？故曰：「樂者，天地之命，中和之紀，人情之所不能免者也。」獨樂其志而不厭其道，備舉其道而不私其欲，則可以達於天下後世矣。茍非身有其德而求之聲容之末，其能淑乎？故兒寬曰：「惟天子建中和之極。」蓋謂此也。當時宣房瓠子之作，天馬寶鼎之歌，亦有協於是否乎？
第貳場
論
萬世不可易之定論
潘龍
translation_en:
…do so; those above act, and the people follow them. When customs are turned back toward simplicity and generosity, could anything fail to undergo a great transformation? The former kings knew that music could not be dispensed with. Thus they grounded it in human feelings and nature, examined its measures and numerical proportions, and established instruction to show the way toward the highest standard. They expanded its rhythms and moderated its embellishments, establishing gradations to promote the practice of deference. Profound virtue is its guiding cord; extended throughout the vastness of all regions, its power to move human hearts is virtually inexhaustible. Deeds and conduct are represented in it [?]; made manifest to distant generations, would its improvement of customs ever come to an end [?]? If the sages had created music to bring the feelings of all under Heaven into balance but had not established it as a means of instruction, its Way might well have fallen into abeyance. How, then, could virtue be discerned through it? Thus it is said: “Music is the mandate of Heaven and Earth, the ordering principle of equilibrium and harmony, and something human feelings cannot do without.” Taking joy in its purpose without ever tiring of its Way, fully putting that Way into practice without making it serve private desires: through these means it can reach all under Heaven and later generations. If one does not possess its virtue oneself but seeks it in the superficial details of sound and outward form, can one bring about moral improvement? Thus Ni Kuan said: “Only the Son of Heaven establishes the highest standard of equilibrium and harmony.” This, presumably, is what he meant. Did the compositions on Xuanfang and Huzi, and the songs of the Heavenly Horse and the Precious Tripod, accord with this principle or not?
Second Session
Discourse
A Definitive Judgment That Cannot Be Altered for Ten Thousand Generations
Pan Long

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭關　批〔古意古體而變化抑揚不爲本文窘束無古人之智次學實者不能到〕
奇士奇士
考試官教諭文　批〔不費繁文而本等詞理自然充暢有體製有精神讀之可以一倡三嘆〕
敬服敬服
考試官學正王　批〔意精格古詞氣渾成而光彩爛然一洗時陋允稱高論〕
天下大器也王天下之大器至難也以天下之
===
大器相傳至重也夫惟知其難且重也在於一
人而教養之必愼逸豫之必防使繼體嗣世靡
有忝德則以之凝天命奠民生承隆茂之業而
垂無疆之休也不難矣爲天下慮者宜於此焉
先之今夫百穀草木皆有本也物而無本不可
固也而况國乎太子者天下之本也侯衛藩屛
則其標幹也保世滋大胥將係焉而可易視之
乎此明王之所爲留意而忠臣哲士之所尤拳
拳也嗚呼賈誼教養太子之言可謂至矣誠萬
punctuated:
同考試官教諭關　批〔古意古體，而變化抑揚，不爲本文窘束。無古人之智次學實者不能到。〕奇士！奇士！
考試官教諭文　批〔不費繁文，而本等詞理自然充暢，有體製，有精神，讀之可以一倡三嘆。〕敬服！敬服！
考試官學正王　批〔意精格古，詞氣渾成，而光彩爛然，一洗時陋，允稱高論。〕
天下，大器也。王天下之大器，至難也；以天下之大器相傳，至重也。夫惟知其難且重也，在於一人，而教養之必愼，逸豫之必防，使繼體嗣世靡有忝德，則以之凝天命、奠民生、承隆茂之業，而垂無疆之休也，不難矣。爲天下慮者，宜於此焉先之。今夫百穀草木，皆有本也。物而無本，不可固也，而况國乎？太子者，天下之本也；侯衛藩屛，則其標幹也。保世滋大，胥將係焉，而可易視之乎？此明王之所爲留意，而忠臣哲士之所尤拳拳也。嗚呼！賈誼教養太子之言，可謂至矣！誠萬
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Guan, Instructor, comments: 〔“Ancient in conception and form, yet varied in movement and cadence, it is not constrained by the source text. Without the wisdom of the ancients and substantial learning [?], one could not attain this.”〕 An extraordinary talent! An extraordinary talent!

Examiner Wen, Instructor, comments: 〔“Without resorting to elaborate writing, its appropriate language and reasoning naturally achieve fullness and fluency. It has form and spirit; reading it, one may sing once and sigh three times in admiration.”〕 My admiration! My admiration!

Examiner Wang, School Director, comments: 〔“Refined in conception and antique in style, its language and force form a seamless whole, radiant with brilliance. It sweeps away the vulgar habits of the age and truly deserves to be called an elevated discourse.”〕

All under Heaven is a great vessel. To rule this great vessel of all under Heaven is supremely difficult; to transmit this great vessel of all under Heaven to a successor is a matter of the utmost gravity. Only when one understands this difficulty and gravity, and that they rest upon a single person, will one necessarily take care in his education and nurture and guard against his indulgence in ease and pleasure. If the successor to the throne and dynasty brings no dishonor upon its virtue, it will then be no difficult matter through him to secure Heaven’s Mandate, establish the people’s livelihood, inherit a flourishing enterprise, and bequeath blessings without limit. Those who take thought for all under Heaven should give this priority.

Now, the many grains, grasses, and trees all have roots. A thing without roots cannot stand firm; how much more is this true of a state! The heir apparent is the root of all under Heaven; the lords who guard and screen the realm are its branches and trunk. Preserving the dynasty through the generations and increasing its greatness will depend upon them all. Can they be treated lightly? This is what enlightened kings attend to, and what loyal ministers and wise men hold especially close to their hearts. Alas! Jia Yi’s words on educating and nurturing the heir apparent may be called consummate indeed! Truly, for ten thousand …

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
世不可易之定論矣在易震爲長子其辭曰震
來虩虩笑言啞啞震驚百里不喪匕鬯夫長子
於天位未復也而聖人教之恐懼以守匕鬯則
長子之所有事也而聖人教之以正位凝命何
哉蓋君人者天下之主也而太子則君之貳也
承鴻業而有之非徒崇高富貴之而已也亦將
投之至艱而貽以重責焉耳經紀民物協和上
下儀刑百辟昭格冢神皆一人之繇也而可不
慎乎今夫鄙庶之家百金之產欲以授其子猶
===
必教之堂構教之播穫不敢輕也而況付百千
萬此者乎一或不戒將可虞者至矣先王知其
然是故太子之生也舉必有禮見於南郊言有
天也過廟則下過闕則趨言有親也蓋自未有
識而教固已行矣猶以爲未也師道之教訓保
保其身體傅傅其德義立之三少明孝仁禮義
以道習之擇孝悌博聞有道術者以衛翼之左
右前後罔非正人如此而教固已備矣然猶以
爲未也長而入學上親而貴仁上齒而貴信上
punctuated:
世不可易之定論矣。在《易》，震爲長子，其辭曰：「震來虩虩，笑言啞啞。震驚百里，不喪匕鬯。」夫長子於天位未復也，而聖人教之恐懼以守；匕鬯則長子之所有事也，而聖人教之以正位凝命，何哉？蓋君人者，天下之主也，而太子則君之貳也。承鴻業而有之，非徒崇高富貴之而已也，亦將投之至艱而貽以重責焉耳。經紀民物，協和上下，儀刑百辟，昭格冢神，皆一人之繇也，而可不慎乎？今夫鄙庶之家，百金之產欲以授其子，猶必教之堂構，教之播穫，不敢輕也，而況付百千萬此者乎？一或不戒，將可虞者至矣。

先王知其然，是故太子之生也，舉必有禮。見於南郊，言有天也；過廟則下，過闕則趨，言有親也。蓋自未有識，而教固已行矣。猶以爲未也，師道之教訓，保保其身體，傅傅其德義，立之三少，明孝仁禮義，以道習之，擇孝悌博聞有道術者以衛翼之，左右前後罔非正人。如此而教固已備矣，然猶以爲未也。長而入學，上親而貴仁，上齒而貴信，上
translation_en:
…an established judgment that cannot be altered for ten thousand generations. In the Book of Changes, Zhen, Thunder, represents the eldest son. Its judgment reads: “Thunder comes: fear and trembling; then laughter and talk, merry and free. Thunder startles a hundred li, yet he does not lose the sacrificial spoon and wine.” The eldest son has not yet assumed the heavenly throne [?], yet the sage teaches him to preserve it through fear and vigilance. The sacrificial spoon and wine belong to the eldest son’s duties, yet the sage teaches him to rectify his position and secure Heaven’s mandate. Why is this? The ruler is master of all under Heaven, and the heir apparent is the ruler’s deputy. To inherit and possess the great enterprise is not merely to be exalted in wealth and rank; it is also to be plunged into the greatest difficulties and entrusted with weighty responsibilities. Ordering the people and all things, bringing harmony to those above and below, serving as a model for the many lords, and illustriously reaching the great spirits—all are the responsibility of the one man, the ruler. How could he fail to exercise care? Even an ordinary household of humble standing, wishing to hand property worth a hundred gold pieces to its son, must teach him to build upon its foundations and to sow and reap; it dares not take the matter lightly. How much more so when entrusting him with a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand times as much! Should vigilance falter even once, the consequences to be feared would be extreme.

The former kings understood this. Thus, from the heir apparent’s birth, every action had its prescribed rites. He was presented at the southern suburban altar to signify that Heaven stood above him. When passing the ancestral temple he dismounted, and when passing the palace gate towers he quickened his steps, to signify that he had parents to honor. His education was thus already under way before he possessed understanding. Yet they still considered this insufficient. The Grand Preceptor guided him with instruction; the Grand Guardian safeguarded his person; and the Grand Mentor cultivated his virtue and righteousness. They appointed the Three Junior Officials for him, made clear filial piety, benevolence, ritual propriety, and righteousness, and trained him in the Way. They selected men who were filial and respectful toward their elders, widely learned, and versed in the Way and its practices, to protect and assist him. To his left and right, before and behind him, there were none but upright men. In this way his education was already fully provided for, yet they still considered this insufficient. When he grew older, he entered school, honoring kinship and esteeming benevolence, honoring seniority and esteeming trustworthiness, honoring…

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
賢而貴德上貴而尊爵承師問道退習而考焉
罰其不則而匡其不逮朝日夕月明有敬也親
饋國老明有孝也行步必節明有度也食遂庖
厨明有仁也然猶恐其非僻之萌也瞽史誦詩
工誦箴諫大夫進謀士傳民語不幸而至於有
失則史記其過宰徹其膳進善有旌誹謗有木
敢諫有鼓則是爲太子者不得一息而肆也夫
人孰不憚檢制而樂縱逸憙媮佚而惡正直哉
而先王之教也必爲其所不快豈其忍於子而
===
靳於愛哉蓋嬰兒剔首而搁痤也必號呼不已
而慈母必且爲之則以犯其所小苦而致其所
大利云耳又况凡人之情養之以豫則耳目不
奸開之以漸則法義易入故童蒙之吉養正之
功聖人蓋言之詳矣是故教之成也以知則明
以性則達以天德則全以王道則備是故以之
導民而從以之宰物而當以之刑百辟而化以
之祀鬼神而享以之昭上下而格參賛位育猶
將致之而况於定天下乎夫然後膺天保之福
punctuated: 賢而貴德，上貴而尊爵，承師問道，退習而考焉。罰其不則而匡其不逮。朝日夕月，明有敬也；親饋國老，明有孝也；行步必節，明有度也；食遂庖厨，明有仁也。然猶恐其非僻之萌也，瞽史誦詩，工誦箴諫，大夫進謀，士傳民語。不幸而至於有失，則史記其過，宰徹其膳。進善有旌，誹謗有木，敢諫有鼓，則是爲太子者不得一息而肆也。夫人孰不憚檢制而樂縱逸，憙媮佚而惡正直哉？而先王之教也，必爲其所不快，豈其忍於子而靳於愛哉？蓋嬰兒剔首而搁痤也，必號呼不已，而慈母必且爲之，則以犯其所小苦而致其所大利云耳。又况凡人之情，養之以豫則耳目不奸，開之以漸則法義易入。故童蒙之吉，養正之功，聖人蓋言之詳矣。是故教之成也，以知則明，以性則達，以天德則全，以王道則備。是故以之導民而從，以之宰物而當，以之刑百辟而化，以之祀鬼神而享，以之昭上下而格。參賛位育，猶將致之，而况於定天下乎？夫然後膺天保之福
translation_en:
…the worthy and prizes virtue; he honors the eminent and respects rank. He receives instruction from his teachers and asks about the Way, then withdraws to practice and examine what he has learned. His departures from proper standards are punished, and his shortcomings corrected. Paying homage to the sun in the morning and the moon in the evening manifests reverence; personally feeding the elders of the state manifests filial piety; observing due measure in every step manifests restraint; keeping the kitchen at a distance when eating [?] manifests benevolence. Yet, still fearing the first stirrings of perversity and depravity, blind musicians and scribes recite poems, musicians recite admonitions, grand officers offer counsel, and gentlemen transmit the words of the people. Should he unfortunately commit an error, the scribes record his fault and the steward withdraws his meal. There are banners for presenting good counsel, wooden posts for voicing criticism, and drums for those who dare remonstrate. Thus the crown prince cannot indulge himself for even a moment.

Who does not dread restraint and delight in unbridled ease, cherish indolence and dislike uprightness? Yet the former kings’ instruction necessarily subjected their sons to what displeased them. Could this have been because they were cruel to their sons and sparing in affection? When an infant’s head is shaved and its sores scraped [?], it will surely cry out incessantly, yet a loving mother will still see it done: she subjects it to a small pain solely to bring it a great benefit. Moreover, human nature is such that, when nurtured through preventive instruction, the ears and eyes do not stray; when enlightened gradually, it readily admits proper standards and moral principles. Thus the sages have spoken fully of the good fortune attending youthful ignorance and the efficacy of nurturing rectitude.

When this education is complete, understanding is lucid, the inherent nature finds full expression, Heaven’s virtue is whole, and the kingly Way is fully realized. Hence, using this to guide the people, he secures their obedience; to govern affairs, he achieves what is fitting; to serve as a model for the many lords, he transforms them; to sacrifice to ghosts and spirits, he obtains their acceptance; and to manifest his virtue above and below, he reaches them all. He may even attain participation in and assistance with Heaven and Earth’s work of placing all things in their proper positions and nurturing them—how much more, then, can he bring stability to all under Heaven! Only then does he receive the blessings of Heaven’s protection…

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
而延靈長之祚即欲去之不能矣三代所以承
命之術繇此其紀也使禹之後而非啓湯之後
而非太甲周文武之後而非成康則雖至德在
人其歷年之久近孰能必之且成王之賢天下
莫不聞微祿之教聞之既熟及其踐祚也可以
繹矣而召公告之曰若生子罔不在厥初生自
貽哲命周公復訓曰繼自今嗣王無淫于觀于
逸于游于田乃猶爲是諄諄者何耶誠欲其念
天命畏民碞克終允德而不忘師保之教云耳
===
□□□嗣守大訓用敷遺後人休豈獨也哉夫人
性不甚相遠也教之成王則成王矣不成王教
之也則亦非成王矣猶之居齊而齊言居楚而
楚言二者將奚擇乎詩曰貽厥孫謀以燕翼子
此聖王之所以重繼世也亦所以重宗廟社稷
也亦所以重天下生民也誼之言斯其至矣君
人者繹忠智之言鑒於得失之故思無逸之明
戒爲垂裕之永圖使周召史佚各進其忠德成
而天下戴之則可以比三代之隆而基苞桑之
punctuated: 而延靈長之祚，即欲去之，不能矣。三代所以承命之術，繇此其紀也。使禹之後而非啓，湯之後而非太甲，周文武之後而非成康，則雖至德在人，其歷年之久近，孰能必之？且成王之賢，天下莫不聞。微祿之教，聞之既熟，及其踐祚也，可以繹矣。而召公告之曰：「若生子，罔不在厥初生，自貽哲命。」周公復訓曰：「繼自今嗣王，無淫于觀、于逸、于游、于田。」乃猶爲是諄諄者，何耶？誠欲其念天命，畏民碞，克終允德，而不忘師保之教云耳。□□□嗣守大訓，用敷遺後人休，豈獨也哉？夫人性不甚相遠也，教之成王，則成王矣；不成王教之也，則亦非成王矣。猶之居齊而齊言，居楚而楚言，二者將奚擇乎？《詩》曰：「貽厥孫謀，以燕翼子。」此聖王之所以重繼世也，亦所以重宗廟社稷也，亦所以重天下生民也。誼之言，斯其至矣。君人者繹忠智之言，鑒於得失之故，思無逸之明戒，爲垂裕之永圖，使周召史佚各進其忠，德成而天下戴之，則可以比三代之隆，而基苞桑之
translation_en:
…and prolong the enduring blessings of the royal line: even if one wished to cast them off, one could not. The methods by which the Three Dynasties sustained the Mandate took this as their guiding principle. Had Yu been succeeded by someone other than Qi, Tang by someone other than Tai Jia, and Kings Wen and Wu of Zhou by someone other than Kings Cheng and Kang, then, although men of consummate virtue had existed, who could have guaranteed how long their dynasties would endure?

Moreover, everyone under Heaven had heard of King Cheng’s worthiness. He had become thoroughly familiar with the instruction of “Wei Lu” [?], and when he ascended the throne, he could reflect upon it. Yet the Duke of Shao admonished him: “It is like bearing a child: everything depends upon its first days of life, when it secures for itself a wise destiny.” The Duke of Zhou further instructed him: “From this time onward, let the succeeding king indulge neither in spectacles, nor in ease, nor in excursions, nor in hunting.” Why did they still exhort him so earnestly? They truly wished him to remain mindful of Heaven’s Mandate, to fear the people’s formidable power, to persevere to the end in true virtue, and never to forget the instruction of his preceptors and guardians.

[Three illegible characters] continue to uphold the great instructions, thereby bestowing blessings abundantly upon later generations—could this concern him alone? Human natures do not differ very greatly. Educate someone as King Cheng was educated, and he will become a King Cheng; fail to educate him as King Cheng was educated, and he will not become a King Cheng. It is like living in Qi and speaking the language of Qi, or living in Chu and speaking the language of Chu: which of these two will one choose? The Book of Odes says: “He bequeathed plans to his descendants, thereby bringing peace to and sheltering his children.” This is why sage kings attached such importance to succession from one generation to the next; it is also why they attached such importance to the ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain, and to all the people under Heaven. Yi’s words express this to the utmost.

Let the ruler ponder words of loyalty and wisdom, take warning from the causes of success and failure, reflect upon the clear admonitions of ‘Against Idleness,’ and devise lasting plans to leave abundance to posterity. Let men such as the Duke of Zhou, the Duke of Shao, and the Scribe Yi each offer their loyal counsel. Once his virtue is perfected and all under Heaven uphold him, he can match the flourishing ages of the Three Dynasties and lay foundations as firmly rooted as a clump of mulberry trees …

title: 嘉靖十九年山東鄉試錄
text:
業尚何景命之不申哉書曰一人元良萬邦以
貞此之謂也
表
擬宋以胡瑗爲國子監直講謝表〔皇祐四年〕
黃觀
同考試官學正萬　批　〔不刻意駢麗而鋪叙揄〕
〔揚自有典則刻此足以正奇巧之習〕
考試官教諭文　批　〔温潤懇切說出胡瑗心〕
〔意非但工于四六者〕
考試官學正王　批　〔立意措詞最得稱謝之〕
〔體平實中文藻爛然他作鮮及〕
皇祐四年某月某日伏蒙
聖恩以臣爲國子監直講者
聖世弘文國學重化成之本
明王崇教儒紳承寵命之榮譽髦忝就乎陶鎔
師責寔慚于模範
恩逾晉錫感切震驚臣瑗誠惶誠恐稽首頓
首上言伏以東膠肇啓爰咨典樂之官靈
punctuated:
業，尚何景命之不申哉？《書》曰：「一人元良，萬邦以貞。」此之謂也。

表
擬宋以胡瑗爲國子監直講謝表〔皇祐四年〕
黃觀

translation_en:
…an enduring foundation: how, then, could the glorious Mandate fail to be prolonged? The Book of Documents says: “When the one man is supremely good, the myriad states are thereby set right.” This is what it means.

Memorial
A draft memorial of thanks on Hu Yuan’s appointment as Instructor in the Directorate of Education under the Song dynasty. 〔Fourth year of Huangyou [1052].〕
By Huang Guan.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wan, School Instructor: 〔Without deliberately striving for ornate parallel prose, its exposition and praise possess their own classical order. Printing this piece will suffice to correct the habit of pursuing ingenuity and clever embellishment.〕

Comment by Examiner Wen, County School Instructor: 〔Gentle, polished, and earnest, it expresses Hu Yuan’s thoughts and feelings; it does more than display skill in four-and-six-character parallel prose.〕

Comment by Examiner Wang, School Instructor: 〔Its conception and wording suit the form of an expression of thanks exceptionally well. Amid its plainness and solidity, literary brilliance shines forth. Few other compositions equal it.〕

On a certain day of a certain month in the fourth year of Huangyou, I humbly received Your Majesty’s gracious appointment of your servant as Instructor in the Directorate of Education.

In this sage age, literary learning flourishes, and the Imperial University gives weight to the foundation of moral transformation. Our enlightened sovereign honors instruction, and scholars receive the glory of his gracious commands. Unworthily counted among the renowned and outstanding scholars [?], I undertake the work of molding others; charged with teaching, I am truly ashamed of my inadequacy as an exemplar. Your favor exceeds even lavish rewards; my gratitude is profound, and I tremble in astonishment. Your servant Yuan, in utmost fear and trepidation, bows his head to the ground and repeatedly kowtows, submitting these words:
